title: Guided MESA colleague survey

questions.question: Are the benchmark version, set of test problems and method for calculating scores identified?
questions.help: Identify the edition of the benchmark, the problems used, and the scoring method. This asks whether all three are stated, not whether they are good choices.

example.why: The passage identifies original HLE and its 2,500 questions. A judging AI compares responses with reference answers, and accuracy is the percentage marked correct, so both the test and its scoring method are described.

questions.question: Are the ability being tested, the intended AI systems and the intended uses described?
questions.help: Look for the skill being tested, which AI systems the test is intended for, and the proposed uses of its scores. A description of these aims is different from evidence that the test achieves them.

example.why: HLE tests academic knowledge and reasoning in AI systems that handle text or text and images. Its scores are intended to compare these systems on academic questions; they do not by themselves establish research ability or general intelligence.

questions.question: Are the test problems, the information provided and the required answers or actions described?
questions.help: The description should say what the AI receives and what it must produce or do. You do not need to solve the problems yourself.

example.why: The AI receives a question, sometimes with an image, and selects an option or gives a short answer. The evaluation software asks for an explanation, a final answer and a percentage stating confidence.

questions.question: Are the instructions, resources and limits for taking the test described?
questions.help: Testing conditions include instructions, tools, supplied documents, time, allowed attempts, and AI settings. This asks whether relevant conditions are described, not whether every possible condition was studied.

example.why: The software describes the instructions and a temperature setting of zero to reduce randomness. However, the line that sends that setting is disabled in the inspected code, so the description does not establish that it was used.

questions.question: Is it described how answers or actions become scores and how results are presented?
questions.help: Look for the rules that turn responses into points, any averaging or weighting, and how results are shown. Describing a scoring rule does not establish that it is accurate or appropriate.

example.why: An AI judge compares each final answer with a reference, accepting equivalent meanings. The code reports the percentage marked correct, a confidence range and how stated confidence compares with accuracy; describing these calculations does not establish that they work well.

questions.question: Is it explained why the test problems measure the ability the benchmark claims to test?
questions.help: The explanation should link the problems to the claimed skill. Being difficult or requiring specialist knowledge does not by itself establish that a task measures reasoning.

example.why: The paper uses specialist academic questions with definite answers to test knowledge and reasoning that existing AI models struggle with. This explains the choice of tasks, but does not establish coverage of every academic skill.

questions.question: Are the origins and choice of test problems justified for the benchmark’s intended use?
questions.help: Look for reasons for the sources, number, topics, and difficulty of problems in relation to the intended use. Availability alone is not a reason that these problems represent the skill.

example.why: Experts contributed questions, and questions that selected AI models could already answer were screened out. This explains how difficulty was chosen, but does not show that the resulting set represents academic work more generally.

questions.question: Were the test problems and the answers used to mark them checked for errors during development?
questions.help: This asks whether both the problems and the supplied answers used to mark them were examined for mistakes during development. It is separate from testing how new AI responses are marked. Evidence that examination occurred does not establish that every answer is correct; note limits in its coverage when relevant.

example.why: Expert review and organizer approval were followed by two checks of 200 questions each, examining questions and reference answers. The reported 15.4% expert disagreement limits confidence in the answers, but does not negate that checking occurred.

questions.question: Is there evidence that the test problems cover the relevant parts of the ability being claimed?
questions.help: A skill may have several relevant parts. Look for evidence that the selected problems cover the parts included in the claim. A narrow set of problems may fit a narrow claim but not a broader one.

example.why: The questions span many subjects but emphasize mathematics and require definite answers. This covers some academic knowledge and reasoning, while creative work and research without a fixed answer fall outside the format.

questions.question: Is there evidence that the way points are awarded reflects the ability the benchmark is meant to measure?
questions.help: Look for evidence that earning more points means doing better at the intended skill. A fixed scoring rule can work exactly as written while rewarding formatting or other features unrelated to that skill.

example.why: The judge accepts responses that mean the same thing as the reference answer, allowing differences in wording. However, it compares answers without independently solving the problem, so a mistaken reference or judging decision can affect the score.

questions.question: Is there evidence supporting how scores are combined and what any separate scores are said to measure?
questions.help: Look for reasons for combining results, weighting groups, and naming any separate skills. Averaging scores is a calculation; it does not by itself establish that the total measures one ability.

example.why: Every question counts equally toward accuracy, so subjects with more questions contribute more to the total. Results are also reported by subject, but the supplied material does not establish that these subject scores measure separate skills.

questions.question: Was the marking process tested to see whether it awards the right scores consistently?
questions.help: Marking can be done by people, fixed software rules, or another AI. This asks whether that process was tested for correct and consistent marks. Testing that found mistakes still counts as testing. Fixed software rules alone do not show that tests occurred, and evidence of some testing does not establish complete marking accuracy.

example.why: The code shows how the AI judge compares responses with reference answers, but no full comparison with expert marking is supplied. Expert checks of the questions do not establish whether this judge marks AI responses correctly and consistently.

questions.question: Are the comparison points used to explain the scores justified for the claims being made?
questions.help: A comparison point is a human score, another AI score, or a guessing result used to interpret a score. Ask whether it fits the stated claim and conditions. Comparing particular systems does not establish a ranking among all systems or a justified score cutoff for a decision.

example.why: The paper compares AI models on the full question set and separately on questions using only text. These provide context, but no matched group of people takes the whole exam under the same conditions, limiting comparisons with human performance.

questions.question: Was it tested how much the same AI system’s score changes when the benchmark is run more than once?
questions.help: This asks whether the same AI was evaluated repeatedly under the same conditions and score changes were measured. One reported evaluation does not establish whether other evaluations occurred; an explicit statement that only one occurred rules out repetition for that evaluation. Neither establishes that repeated scores would be unstable.

example.why: The paper acknowledges that an AI can answer differently on separate attempts. The supplied sources do not establish repeated testing of the same systems for the main comparisons, so the size of score changes remains unknown.

questions.question: Was it tested how much scores change when instructions, presentation or the testing setup change?
questions.help: This asks whether effects of changed instructions, presentation, or settings were measured. Repeating identical conditions is different from changing conditions. Findings about one change need not cover every possible change.

example.why: The supplied sources do not establish systematic tests of reworded instructions or changes to the judging AI. Describing one instruction and testing setup does not show how much scores change when those conditions change.

questions.question: Are estimates of how much scores could vary provided in enough detail to support the comparisons or decisions being made?
questions.help: Look for a range or other estimate of possible score differences, how it was calculated, and whether it supports the intended comparison. An estimate based on the number of problems need not measure changes across repeated evaluations; small score differences may remain unresolved.

example.why: The code estimates a 95% confidence range from the number of questions and the fraction marked correct. It does not measure changes from rerunning the AI or replacing the judge, so it covers only some uncertainty in comparisons.

questions.question: Were ways of earning points without using the ability being tested investigated?
questions.help: A shortcut earns points without the intended skill, for example through accidental clues. This asks whether such routes were investigated. Identifying a possible shortcut does not establish that a tested AI used it; an investigation that found a problem still occurred.

example.why: Contributors were asked to avoid questions answered by a simple lookup and could revise questions answered through faulty reasoning. These checks address some shortcuts, but guessing remains possible and the supplied material does not measure every route to points.

questions.question: Was the risk that AI systems had already seen the test problems or answers assessed and addressed?
questions.help: Look for both an assessment of earlier exposure to questions or answers and steps to address the risk. Public availability may create a risk without proving that a particular model saw the material. Protective measures do not establish that exposure was impossible.

example.why: A private question set, a text marker identifying test data and warnings against training on the test help address prior exposure. These precautions do not establish which questions or answers any particular AI encountered during training.

questions.question: Are the rules on training specifically for this test and repeatedly submitting results justified for the intended use?
questions.help: Look for rules about training specifically for the test and repeatedly submitting results, with reasons linked to the intended use. A rule being absent from the supplied description is different from evidence that the rule is unsuitable.

example.why: The instructions discourage training on test questions. However, the supplied material lacks a complete policy covering repeated submissions, access to feedback and reporting systems trained for HLE, leaving insufficient information to judge whether the rules support the intended comparisons.

questions.question: Is there evidence for any claim that the scores show how well an AI system will perform beyond the problems in this test?
questions.help: This concerns claims about new problems or real work beyond the benchmark. Look for evidence covering that broader claim. A stated ambition alone is not such evidence; if no broader claim or use arises, consider Not applicable.

example.why: The supplied passage reports no measured relationship between HLE scores and success on independent scientific projects. Academic question scores therefore leave that broader claim unresolved; missing evidence does not prove that an AI cannot conduct research.

questions.question: Is there evidence that comparisons are fair across the AI systems and situations the benchmark is meant to cover?
questions.help: Look for evidence that differences in information, tools, tasks, resources, or settings do not make the intended comparison misleading. Findings about differences between people do not by themselves establish fair comparisons between AI systems.

example.why: Results using only text are labelled separately from results that include images. This helps compare systems receiving similar information, but English questions, unequal subject coverage and missing studies across languages leave other fairness claims unresolved.

questions.question: Are the test materials and methods available in enough detail for someone else to repeat the evaluation or examine how it was done?
questions.help: Look for enough problems, scoring details, instructions, and software to repeat or inspect the evaluation. Public access to some files does not necessarily reproduce hidden test results or earlier software versions.

example.why: The instructions and marking code are public, allowing readers to inspect the procedure. Downloading questions requires accepting access conditions, and a separate private question set is withheld, so not all materials are available to examine or repeat every result.

questions.question: Are the rules for accessing and reusing the benchmark, and the protections needed for responsible use, stated?
questions.help: Look for access and reuse rules and relevant safeguards, such as protecting hidden answers. A missing permission statement does not establish that reuse is prohibited. This asks whether relevant rules are stated, not whether all materials must be public.

example.why: The dataset and code list MIT licences, access requires accepting conditions, and the paper describes excluding dangerous content. However, the dataset also asks users not to redistribute questions, leaving some reuse expectations unclear alongside the licence.

questions.question: Are changes to the benchmark recorded, including how they affect comparisons between old and new scores?
questions.help: Look for a record of changes to problems, answers, or scoring and an explanation of their effects on old and new scores. A new version number alone does not explain whether scores can be compared.

example.why: HLE-Rolling records removed and restored questions, but it is separate from original HLE. The supplied material does not establish how changes to original HLE affect comparisons between earlier and later scores.

questions.question: Do the published claims stay within what the evidence supports?
questions.help: Compare what is publicly claimed with the tasks, conditions, and results actually reported. A claim about these tasks may be justified even when a broader claim is not. Missing evidence for a broad claim does not prove that the AI lacks the ability.

example.why: The paper says high scores alone do not establish general intelligence or independent research ability. However, the title “Humanity’s Last Exam” can suggest broader coverage than a set of academic questions with definite answers supports.

benchmarks.name: ARC-AGI-2
benchmarks.subtitle: Learning rules from coloured grids
benchmarks.scope: ARC-AGI-2 public test problems, the official scoring software, and ARC Prize’s rules for tests that it runs or verifies. Sources were inspected on 7 October 2026. Other competitions and community results may use different rules.
benchmarks.overview: Each puzzle shows several before-and-after grids of coloured squares. The AI must infer the hidden rule and produce outputs for new inputs. Public development tasks are available for practice; separate tasks are used for evaluation. You do not need to solve the puzzles to complete this survey.
benchmarks.intended_use: Using scores to compare AI systems’ ability to solve unfamiliar grid problems, and considering the creators’ broader claims about reasoning.

facts.text: The release lists 1,000 public development tasks and three evaluation sets of 120 tasks each. Exact public-data and scorer versions are identified for this packet; hidden tasks are not supplied.
The stated goal is abstract problem-solving on unfamiliar tasks, requiring little specialist knowledge. The creators connect this to progress toward more general, human-like AI.
Each task gives input/output grid examples and new input grids. The system must supply the missing outputs, including their size and cell colours.
Two attempts are allowed per input. Verified testing specifies model settings and a cost cap; other evaluation routes can differ.

The inspected scorer checks grid equality, averages successes across test inputs within a task, then across tasks. A task with one of two inputs solved receives 0.5. The dataset description calls a task solved only when all inputs are correct.

The creators aim to test learning a new transformation from examples, rather than recalling facts. Their design goals include combining concepts and reducing success through exhaustive trial-and-error search.
Candidates came from newly written tasks and unused reserves. Selection included human trials and removal of tasks judged to test the same rule; evaluation sets were balanced for human difficulty.
The paper describes human solvability checks and additional internal review. The change record later lists corrected cells and ambiguities in some public examples and test outputs.

The test uses two-dimensional grids. Its goals concern abstract reasoning and increasingly complex combinations of concepts. This packet contains no study establishing coverage of language, social interaction or real-world autonomous work.

A submitted grid matches only if its dimensions and cells match the reference. There is no credit for a partly correct grid, though a multi-input task can receive partial credit when some whole grids are correct.

The software averages within tasks and then across tasks. It does not report separate validated ability scores. The dataset’s all-inputs-correct description and software average are both supplied in Q5.

The public repository includes scorer tests for correct answers, wrong dimensions, changed pixels and missing outputs. The packet preparer inspected these cases but did not run a full scorer-validation study.
Human testing involved 407 people in 515 paid, 90-minute sessions on candidate tasks. The final dataset excludes some candidates.
The current verified-testing policy specifies one run rather than an average of runs. This packet includes no repeated-run variation estimates for a fixed AI system and setup.
Runner settings are configurable. The inspected sources provide no systematic study of instruction, representation or software changes.
The report gives model scores without corresponding repeat-run variance or confidence ranges. Human difficulty matching between sets is different.

The design explicitly targets resistance to exhaustive program search. The creators also compare tasks for redundancy. The packet contains no quantified demonstration that all alternative ways to earn credit have been eliminated.
Public tasks are accessible. For hidden remote tests, the policy specifies data-retention agreements and exposure monitoring, and acknowledges possible leakage.

The dataset instructions permit training on development tasks and warn against tuning using evaluation tasks. The verified-testing policy says testing is not a continuous optimization service for providers.
The creators connect performance to more general reasoning. This packet contains no study showing how ARC-AGI-2 scores predict success on other jobs. The reported experiments concern grid tasks.
Recorded human background factors showed no clear statistical relationship with performance. Verified tests record settings; other evaluation routes can differ.

Public data, running software and scorer tests are available. Hidden sets have controlled access. Policy states that public testing outputs, costs, durations and task scores are released; this packet did not audit the complete archive.
Public data carry an Apache 2.0 license. The policy sets restrictions for hidden data and describes confidentiality arrangements, provider handling and code review for selected submissions.

The dated change record identifies corrected tasks and links changes to commits. It does not provide a before-and-after score comparison for every affected model. ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 are separate versions.

Public descriptions use broad language about intelligence while describing a particular family of grid tasks. The information here includes those claims and the study limits; it does not include a universal intelligence score or real-world deployment study.

reading.title: What the AI is asked to do
reading.text: ARC-AGI-2 is a test developed by ARC Prize Foundation staff and partners to assess whether an AI can **work out a new rule from examples**. Each problem presents pairs of coloured grids, showing a starting grid alongside its correct finished grid. Using those examples, the AI must work out how to complete a new starting grid and return an answer with the right size and colour in every square. The creators designed these problems to require little specialist knowledge while encouraging the AI to combine ideas. Their aim is to study reasoning that goes beyond recalling facts or trying large numbers of possible programs, which they connect to progress toward more general, human-like AI.

reading.title: How the problems were chosen
reading.text: ARC-AGI-2’s developers began with a collection of newly written grid puzzles and puzzles prepared for earlier ARC work that had not been used. To help decide which puzzles to include and how difficult they were, the developers **conducted a study in which people tried solving them**. This involved **407 people taking part in 515 paid, 90-minute sessions**. The puzzles used in that study formed a larger pool than the final test, so the results do not all describe the final set. The developers also reviewed puzzles themselves and removed ones they judged could be solved by the same rule. The released benchmark contains **1,000 problems for practice and AI development**, along with **three test sets of 120 problems each**. These sets are called public, semi-private and private because access to their problems differs. Using the human participants’ results, the developers selected the three test sets to have similar difficulty for people. After release, they continued correcting the materials; a public change record lists fixes to some coloured squares and unclear examples.

reading.title: How answers earn points
reading.text: The AI is allowed **two attempts for each new input grid**, and it earns credit for that input only if an attempt matches the supplied answer in both size and every square’s colour. A nearly correct grid therefore receives no credit. A problem can contain several new inputs, however, so the official scoring software inspected for this survey calculates the fraction solved within each problem before averaging the problem scores. Solving one of two inputs, for example, earns **0.5 for that problem**. This differs from calling the whole problem “fully solved,” which the instructions published with the problems reserve for cases where every input is correct. The software does not provide separate scores established as measures of distinct skills. Its public tests cover correct answers, wrong sizes, changed squares and missing outputs; the survey preparer inspected those tests without independently testing the whole marking system.

reading.title: Testing conditions and changes in scores
reading.text: ARC Prize, the organization running the verified evaluations, specifies AI settings and a spending limit for the tests it verifies, although other testing routes may use different conditions. Its verified-testing policy uses **one run, rather than an average of repeated runs**. A technical report describing ARC-AGI-2’s development gives AI scores, but the materials reviewed here do not provide estimates or ranges showing how much the same AI’s score changes when the same test is repeated. Although the running software allows settings to be changed, those materials also contain no systematic study of the effects of changing instructions, grid presentation or software. Matching the test sets for human difficulty addresses a separate issue and does not measure these changes in AI scores.

reading.title: Prior exposure and ways to earn points
reading.text: The creators tried to limit ways of earning points without the intended reasoning by designing problems that resist searches through large numbers of possible programs and by checking for repeated solution rules. These steps do not establish that every such route to a high score has been ruled out. Prior exposure is another concern because anyone can see the public problems. For hidden tests sent to AI providers, ARC Prize describes agreements against retaining the data and monitoring of possible exposure, while acknowledging that information could still escape. To keep development separate from evaluation, **training on development problems is allowed, while changing a system specifically to improve on evaluation problems is discouraged**. ARC Prize also says its verified tests are not a service for repeatedly improving systems through its feedback.

reading.title: Comparisons, access and updates
reading.text: In the puzzle-solving study described above, the developers found no clear statistical relationship between performance and recorded background factors such as work and technical experience. For AI comparisons, verified tests record the settings used, though other testing routes may differ. Researchers can inspect **public problems, running software and marking tests**, while access to hidden problems is controlled. ARC Prize says it also releases public testing outputs, costs, times and problem scores, but the survey preparer did not check the complete archive. The public data use an Apache 2.0 licence; hidden-data rules address confidentiality, provider handling and code review for selected submissions. To help track revisions, a dated change record identifies corrected problems and exact code changes. It does not, however, recalculate every affected AI score, and ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 remain separate test versions.

reading.title: What the findings cover
reading.text: Although the creators connect ARC-AGI-2 to abstract reasoning and broader intelligence, the studies supplied here concern **two-dimensional grid problems**. This packet contains no study showing how scores predict success in language, social interaction or other real-world work, and it supplies no measure covering every kind of intelligence. These are **limits of the information available for this survey**: they leave those broader relationships unresolved, rather than showing that such relationships are impossible.

steps.title: Input 2: unsolved

benchmarks.name: DesignQA
benchmarks.subtitle: Understanding engineering rules and drawings
benchmarks.overview: The AI receives written engineering rules, vehicle images or drawings and must answer questions about them. It may need to find a rule, explain a technical term, identify a part, or check whether a design meets a requirement. The questions draw on Formula SAE, a competition in which university students design and build racing cars. You do not need engineering knowledge or to solve these problems to review this test.
benchmarks.scope: The original DesignQA benchmark described in the 2024 paper, together with its public scoring software. Sources were inspected on 6 October 2026. Later changes to the questions or software may affect results.
benchmarks.intended_use: Using scores to compare how well AI systems find and apply engineering rules and understand vehicle drawings, while considering how far these results support claims about understanding other engineering documents.

reading.title: What the AI is asked to do
reading.text: DesignQA was created by researchers and engineers working with materials from **Formula SAE, a competition in which university students design and build racing cars**. Their aim was to test whether an AI can find engineering rules, understand technical terms and drawings, and apply rules to a design. The paper describes **1,451 question-and-answer pairs in six groups**. These ask the AI to find an individual rule, gather related rules, explain a technical term, identify whether a component is present, check dimensions, or assess performance against a requirement. Depending on the question, the AI receives written rules, a vehicle image or a drawing and must give a text answer or a yes/no answer, sometimes with an explanation. These tasks follow parts of an engineer’s work, which is the authors’ reason for using them to assess understanding of engineering documents.

reading.title: How the questions were chosen and checked
reading.text: The developers used a real competition rulebook, vehicle designs and test data, drawing on contributions from engineering practitioners and researchers. This gives the questions a clear connection to practical work, but the benchmark uses **one rulebook and a limited range of tasks**, rather than a representative sample of engineering work across industries. The groups are also very uneven: finding individual rules accounts for 1,192 questions, while checking functional performance accounts for only 16. The paper reports that two additional reviewers checked manually written questions, with exceptions for questions derived from others and some explanations. Those explanations received a more limited check that they supported the yes/no answer. The reviewed sources do not establish how often reviewers disagreed or how many errors remained.

reading.title: How answers earn points
reading.text: DesignQA uses several marking methods because its questions require different kinds of answers. Some methods compare the wording of an AI answer with a supplied answer, while yes/no questions receive credit for the correct decision and may also have their explanations scored for text similarity. These rules are described, but **wording and formatting can affect credit**: the paper gives examples involving missing commas and valid related rules that were absent from the supplied answer. The public software also produces an overall score by giving each of the six question groups equal weight, despite their different sizes and marking methods. The reviewed material does not show that this overall number, or the separate group scores, measures a distinct underlying skill. Small marking-test files and discussion of scoring problems show some checking, but do not establish a complete study of marking accuracy and consistency.

reading.title: Testing conditions and comparisons
reading.text: The paper names the AI systems tested and describes instructions and settings, but **not every system receives the same information**. Some receive the whole rulebook, while others receive passages selected by search software. Their results therefore describe the AI together with its information supply, which matters when comparing systems. The authors include results from random guessing and other AI systems, but no reported baseline from human engineers taking the test. They also examine changes in the supplied passages, dimension labels, scale bars and highlighted images. One AI is tested with five different sets of rule passages, providing some information about variation. Because the passages change, this does not isolate variation when an identical test is repeated. For the main model comparisons, the reported information is insufficient to judge small score differences confidently. In the 16-question performance group, for example, one additional correct answer changes accuracy by 6.25 percentage points.

reading.title: Prior exposure and unintended ways to earn points
reading.text: The authors discuss influences such as formatting, wording, the quality of retrieved passages and familiarity with components. This shows attention to some factors beyond engineering understanding, but the reviewed material does not fully test ways of gaining points without that understanding. For example, the described drawings with scale bars all comply with the relevant rule. A reviewer can therefore infer that always answering “yes” would earn the yes/no credit on that portion, although this **does not show that any tested AI used that strategy**. The authors also discuss the novelty of their vehicle images and possible exposure to similar images, without directly checking every AI’s training data. The rulebook and released questions are public, and a protected test set or systematic overlap check was not established in the review. Clear enough rules on training on the questions and repeatedly submitting results were also not available in the sources examined.

reading.title: Available materials and later changes
reading.text: Public questions, instructions, scoring code and some AI responses allow researchers to inspect parts of the evaluation. However, they do not provide **a complete record for repeating every result in the paper**: the exact historical software, settings and inputs are not fully linked to each result. One released answer file also contains fewer rows than the corresponding question count in the paper. Code history makes revisions identifiable, but the reviewer did not find a clear change record explaining their effects on scores, a licence file, or complete rules for responsible reuse. These findings describe limits of the materials inspected; they do not establish that permission is unavailable elsewhere or that reuse is prohibited.

reading.title: What the results can support
reading.text: DesignQA’s paper acknowledges the limits of using one rulebook, a small set of task types and imperfect marking methods. It also says that **performance on a different technical document remains uncertain**. Real vehicle materials make the test relevant to engineering, but they do not demonstrate that its scores predict success on other standards or real engineering projects. The completed review below therefore treats the benchmark as a way to examine performance on these tasks under stated conditions. Broader claims about engineering competence, or fine distinctions between closely ranked systems, require more support.

terms: Benchmark
A test used to assess an AI system.
Benchmark version
A particular edition or revision of a test. Its problems, answers or marking rules may differ from an earlier edition. The edition matters when comparing scores.
Ability or skill
Something the AI is meant to be able to do, such as finding a rule in a pattern or answering a science question. A score on one skill does not automatically describe every skill.
AI system or model
The software taking the test, sometimes with extra tools.
Task, item or test problem
One question or puzzle the AI must solve.
Prompt
The instructions and information given to the AI.
Reference answer
The supplied answer used to mark the AI’s response.
Score
The result of marking, such as percentage correct.
Evaluation set
The group of problems used to test a system. A separate development set may be used to improve it.
Scoring software or harness
Code that calculates scores or runs the test.
Score uncertainty
How uncertain a score estimate is under the method used to calculate it. This is different from the AI saying it is confident.
Intended use
The claim or decision a score is meant to support.
paper_title: MESA: Adapting and Testing an EFPA-Based Framework for AI Benchmark Review
introduction: This survey introduces MESA, the Meta-Evaluation Standard for AI Benchmarks. MESA helps people review how an AI test is designed and what its scores can tell us. You will first describe your familiarity with a few relevant ideas, then read an answered example about Humanity’s Last Exam. After that, you will make your own judgments about ARC-AGI-2 and DesignQA.

example.name: Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)
example.subtitle: Advanced academic questions with definite answers
example.scope: The original 2,500-question HLE described in the supplied paper, with the simple public evaluation code inspected on 7 October 2026. This survey does not cover HLE-Rolling, HLE-Diamond or their evaluations with extra tools.
example.overview: Imagine a very difficult exam assembled by specialists from many subjects. The AI must select an answer or give a short answer; some questions also include an image. A separate AI marks the response against a supplied answer. HLE aims to measure advanced academic knowledge and reasoning. You do not need to know the subject answers to evaluate how this test is built, marked and interpreted.
example.intended_use: Using scores to compare AI systems on difficult academic questions, and considering claims about academic expertise beyond the exact questions.

facts.text: This section concerns original HLE: the 2,500-question public test described in the supplied paper. Public grading scripts are pinned for this packet. HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond are separate versions and are not the test being rated.

The authors aim to assess advanced academic knowledge and reasoning on questions with specific answers. They target language and image-capable AI systems, for capability measurement and research communication.

Questions span many academic subjects. About 24% are multiple-choice; the remainder require short answers. About 14% use images. A published biology example asks for a number about the anatomy of a hummingbird bone. No biology expertise is needed for this survey.

The supplied prediction script asks for an explanation, final answer and confidence percentage, and sends images when present. The README describes a default temperature of zero; in the inspected API call, the temperature-setting line is commented out. This packet concerns the simple evaluation, not tool-assisted HLE-Diamond.

An AI judge compares final answers with references, allowing equivalent forms. The script reports percentage correct, a confidence range, and how closely the AI’s stated confidence matches correctness.
The authors use expert-written, difficult questions with known answers to test academic knowledge and reasoning. They explicitly distinguish answering such questions from doing open-ended research.

Experts from many institutions supplied questions. Questions already answered by selected contemporary models were screened out before expert review. The resulting set was selected for difficulty, not randomly sampled from everyday academic work.

The paper describes expert review, organizer approval and audits. Appendix B.3 reports two 200-question audits and an estimated 15.4% expert-disagreement rate after the second. Disagreement is not the same as a confirmed wrong-answer rate.
The paper groups questions across numerous subjects and emphasizes mathematics. The accepted formats require definite answers. Open-ended research and creative work are outside the tested format.
The judge checks meaningful agreement with the reference, without re-solving the problem. This does not settle whether a disputed reference is correct.
Accuracy counts correct answers equally; subject mix therefore affects the overall score. Category results are reported, without a separate-ability validation study in the inspected material.
Judge software is public. Question audits are not automated-marking checks. No full judge-versus-expert agreement study was identified in the inspected sources.

The paper compares several named AI models and reports full-set and text-only results. Question contributors are experts, but this packet contains no matched human cohort taking the entire exam under the model-testing conditions.

The paper notes that a model can answer differently across attempts. The inspected sources do not provide a repeated-run stability study covering the main reported model comparisons. A generation-setting value alone is not a measurement of repeatability.

The paper supplies a standard response prompt and separates full-set from text-only results. This packet includes no systematic experiment measuring score changes after rewording prompts or changing grading-model versions.
The script’s approximate 95% range uses question count and fraction correct, not repeated AI runs or judge versions. Its separate calibration measure compares stated confidence with correctness.

Contributors were asked to avoid easy lookup and could modify questions when models guessed correctly with faulty reasoning. Multiple-choice options still allow guessing. No comprehensive study quantifying every possible shortcut is supplied here.

Authors retain a private set to assess overfitting. The public release includes a distinctive marker to help exclude it from future training, plus a warning against training on the test. Neither measure demonstrates what any particular model actually saw.

The repository warns against including benchmark data in training. The packet supplies no complete original-HLE rule set on repeated submissions, feedback access or separation of results from systems tuned on the test.

The paper says high scores concern closed-ended academic questions, not proof of autonomous research or general intelligence. This packet includes no measured relationship between HLE scores and success in independent scientific projects.

Image-capable and text-only systems do not necessarily receive the same question set. The paper labels text-only results. Questions are written in English and subject coverage is uneven. No comprehensive cross-language or cross-population comparison study is supplied here.

Public instructions and grading code are available. The dataset page requires accepting contact-sharing conditions before file access. The private set is not released. This packet was prepared without downloading gated questions or reproducing the model results.

The dataset page labels its license MIT and presents an access gate and a request not to redistribute test data. The code has an MIT license. The paper excludes certain dangerous-content categories during question collection. These are stated terms and precautions, not a legal assessment.

The site distinguishes original HLE, HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond. A separate rolling log records removals and re-additions. Those changes do not automatically describe original HLE, and this packet supplies no score-equivalence study across all versions.

The title suggests a final exam at the frontier of human knowledge. The paper narrows its interpretation to specific academic answers and explicitly says high performance alone would not establish autonomous research or general intelligence.

reading.title: What the AI is asked to do
reading.text: Humanity’s Last Exam, or HLE, aims to assess advanced academic knowledge and reasoning in AI systems that handle text or text and images. This survey focuses on **the original HLE, which contains 2,500 difficult questions**, rather than the separate HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond versions. About **24% of its questions are multiple-choice**, while the rest require short answers, and about **14% include an image**. A published biology example asks for a number about the anatomy of a hummingbird bone. You do not need to solve that problem to complete this survey; it illustrates the kind of specialist question the AI receives. Across these formats, HLE asks for specific answers rather than the completion of an open-ended research project.

reading.title: How the questions were chosen and checked
reading.text: Experts from many institutions contributed questions covering a range of subjects, with particular emphasis on mathematics. Before expert review, questions that selected AI models could already answer were screened out, so the resulting set was **deliberately chosen to be difficult**, rather than randomly drawn from everyday academic work. HLE’s creators describe their development process in a research paper, which reports expert review and organizer approval, followed by two further checks of 200 questions each. After the second check, the authors estimated an **expert-disagreement rate of 15.4%**. That figure concerns disagreements about questions or answers; it should not be read as the percentage confirmed to be wrong. Because the test requires specific answers, it also leaves creative work and open-ended research outside its answer format.

reading.title: Instructions and marking
reading.text: HLE’s public evaluation software gives the AI each question, includes an image when needed, and asks it to return an explanation, a final answer and a percentage stating its confidence. The instructions for that software describe a default “temperature” of zero, a setting intended to reduce randomness, but the line that sends this setting is **disabled in the inspected code**. Once a response is produced, a separate **AI judge compares the final answer with the supplied reference answer**, accepting different wording when the meaning is the same. Because the judge is instructed to compare answers rather than solve the problem independently, agreement does not establish that the reference itself is correct. The judging code is public, but the inspected sources contain no full study comparing its marks with expert marks. The expert reviews of the questions described earlier therefore do not, by themselves, establish that the automatic marking is accurate.

reading.title: What the reported numbers mean
reading.text: HLE reports **accuracy as the percentage of answers marked correct**, with each question counting equally. As a result, the mix of subjects affects the total score. The paper also reports results by subject, although the inspected material does not establish that these are separate measures of distinct skills. Alongside accuracy, the public scoring software calculates an **approximate 95% confidence range** using the number of questions and the fraction marked correct. This range describes score uncertainty under the calculation’s assumptions; it does not measure the effects of repeating the AI run or changing the judge. A separate calculation compares the AI’s stated confidence with how often its answers are correct, so **confidence in an answer and uncertainty in a test score refer to different things**.

reading.title: Comparisons and repeated testing
reading.text: To put results in context, the paper compares named AI models and reports scores for both the full question set and text-only questions. Although experts helped create the questions, this packet contains **no matched group of people taking the whole exam under the AI testing conditions**. The paper also notes that an AI can answer differently on different attempts, but the inspected sources do not provide a repeated-run study covering the main comparisons. Nor do they provide a systematic study of reworded instructions or changes to the judging AI. Using a fixed setting or a standard instruction therefore does not, on its own, establish how stable the reported scores are.

reading.title: Prior exposure and ways to earn points
reading.text: To reduce easy ways of gaining points, contributors were asked to avoid questions answerable by a simple lookup and could revise questions when an AI guessed correctly through faulty reasoning. Multiple-choice questions still allow guessing, however, and the supplied material does not measure every possible way of earning points without the intended knowledge or reasoning. The authors also retain a **private test set** to help assess whether improvements are specific to the public questions. For the public data, a distinctive text marker helps people identify material to exclude from future AI training, while the instructions warn against training on the test. These precautions do not establish what a particular AI has already seen. The packet also lacks a complete original-HLE policy covering repeated submissions, access to feedback and the reporting of systems trained specifically on the test.

reading.title: Access, fair comparisons and updates
reading.text: Fair comparisons depend partly on which questions each system receives. Systems that use images and those that only use text do not necessarily answer the same set, so the paper labels text-only results. The questions are in English and subjects are not equally represented; the supplied material contains no comprehensive study of comparisons across languages or populations. Public instructions and marking code allow some inspection, but downloading the dataset requires accepting contact-sharing conditions, and the private set is not released. The dataset page lists an MIT licence and asks users not to redistribute test data, while the code also has an MIT licence. The authors describe excluding certain kinds of dangerous content during collection. The survey preparer inspected the available documentation without downloading the gated questions or rerunning the AI evaluations. When comparing results over time, the edition also matters: HLE-Rolling has its own record of removed and restored questions, and **those changes do not automatically describe original HLE**. No study establishing equivalent scores across original HLE, HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond is supplied here.

reading.title: What the findings cover
reading.text: HLE’s title suggests a final exam at the edge of human knowledge, but the paper limits its interpretation to difficult academic questions with definite answers. It explicitly states that **a high score alone does not establish general intelligence or the ability to conduct independent research**. Consistent with that limit, this packet contains no measured relationship between HLE scores and success on independent scientific projects. Such gaps leave broader claims unresolved; they do not, by themselves, show that the benchmark fails.

familiarity.question: How familiar are you with AI?
familiarity.help: Think about your experience using or learning about AI, such as a chatbot. This is your own description, not a knowledge test.
labels: 1 — New to me: I have little or no experience with AI.
2 — A little familiar: I have heard about or tried AI.
3 — Somewhat familiar: I use AI sometimes and understand its basic purpose.
4 — Familiar: I use AI regularly and understand some of its limits.
5 — Very familiar: I can explain how AI is used and discuss its limits confidently.

familiarity.question: How familiar are you with AI benchmarks?
familiarity.help: An AI benchmark is a test used to assess an AI system. Think about how familiar this idea was before reading this survey.
labels: 1 — New to me: I had not heard of AI benchmarks.
2 — A little familiar: I had heard the term but could not explain it.
3 — Somewhat familiar: I knew that benchmarks test AI and produce scores.
4 — Familiar: I knew how some benchmark problems and scores are used.
5 — Very familiar: I could explain benchmarks and discuss what their scores can and cannot show.

familiarity.question: How confident are you about interpreting AI test scores?
familiarity.help: Interpreting a score means deciding what a result tells us, such as whether two AI systems can be compared fairly. Choose how confident you feel now.
labels: 1 — Not confident: I would need help understanding a test score.
2 — Slightly confident: I understand a simple score but need help comparing results.
3 — Moderately confident: I can explain a basic score and recognize some limits.
4 — Confident: I can compare results and explain important limits.
5 — Very confident: I can explain why a comparison is fair or uncertain and what evidence is needed.

definitions.label: AI
definitions.definition: Software that can perform tasks such as answering questions or working with text and images. The software taking a test may also use extra tools.

definitions.label: AI benchmark
definitions.definition: A test used to assess an AI system. It contains problems, a way to mark answers and rules for interpreting results.

definitions.label: Benchmark version
definitions.definition: A particular edition of a test. Its problems, answers or marking rules may differ from another edition, so the edition matters when comparing scores.

definitions.label: Test problem
definitions.definition: One question or puzzle that the AI must answer or solve.

definitions.label: Ability
definitions.definition: Something the AI is meant to be able to do, such as finding a pattern or answering a science question. Doing well on one skill does not automatically show every skill.

definitions.label: Score
definitions.definition: The result of marking answers, such as the percentage correct. A score has meaning only in relation to the test and the conditions used.

definitions.label: Scoring
definitions.definition: The rules or software that turn an AI’s answers into points or a result.

definitions.label: Reference answer
definitions.definition: The supplied answer against which the AI’s response is marked. It can be wrong, so agreement with it is not proof that it is correct.

definitions.label: Prompt
definitions.definition: The directions and information given to the AI before it answers.

definitions.label: Score uncertainty
definitions.definition: How much a score estimate could vary under the assumptions of a calculation. It differs from the AI saying it is confident about an answer.

definitions.label: Intended use
definitions.definition: The comparison, claim or decision that a score is meant to support.

definitions.label: AI judge
definitions.definition: Another AI that marks a response by following instructions, often by comparing it with a supplied answer. Its marking can also make mistakes.

definitions.label: Comparison point
definitions.definition: A result used to help interpret a score, such as random guessing, a person’s score or another AI’s score.

definitions.label: Repeated testing
definitions.definition: Running the same test more than once to see whether the scores change.

definitions.label: Prior exposure
definitions.definition: The possibility that an AI encountered a test question or answer before taking the test, for example during its training.

definitions.label: Development
definitions.definition: The process of creating, selecting and checking the test problems and scoring rules.

definitions.label: Training
definitions.definition: The process in which an AI learns from data before it is used. If test answers are included, later test scores may reflect earlier exposure.

definitions.label: Evaluation set
definitions.definition: The collection of problems used to assess an AI. It may be separate from problems available for practice.

definitions.label: Open-ended research
definitions.definition: Work where the answer or next step is not fixed in advance, such as investigating a new scientific question.

definitions.label: General intelligence
definitions.definition: A broad ability to handle many different kinds of problems. A high score on one test does not establish this by itself.

definitions.label: Published
definitions.definition: Made available for others to read, for example in a paper, website or report. Publication alone does not mean the information has been checked.

definitions.label: Claim
definitions.definition: Something stated about what a benchmark measures or what its results show. For example, that a score shows an AI can reason.

definitions.label: Evidence
definitions.definition: Information used to judge whether a claim is supported, such as results from tests, comparisons or checks. Evidence can have limits and does not always settle the question.

definitions.label: Comparison
definitions.definition: Looking at results side by side, such as scores from two AI systems, to see how they differ. Differences in test questions or testing conditions can affect what the comparison tells us.

definitions.label: Protection
definitions.definition: Measures intended to prevent harm when accessing or using a benchmark, such as protecting private information or restricting access to content that could cause harm.

definitions.label: Test materials
definitions.definition: The questions, images, files and reference answers used in the benchmark.

definitions.label: Methods
definitions.definition: The procedures used to run the benchmark, mark responses and calculate results.

definitions.label: Situation
definitions.definition: The circumstances in which an AI is tested or used, such as the language, subject area, available tools or testing conditions.

definitions.label: Repeatedly submitting results
definitions.definition: Sending results for the same benchmark more than once, for example after changing an AI system. If feedback guides those changes, later scores may reflect adaptation to that test.

answer_instructions: Yes: information supports the whole condition. Partly: supports some parts but not all. No: information shows the condition is not met. Not sure: information is missing, unclear, or insufficient. Not applicable: the issue does not apply. For a question asking whether checking or testing occurred, Yes means the stated checks occurred for all parts of the question, not that results were favourable or every error was eliminated. Partly means that only some of those checks or parts are supported. Describe limits in coverage in an optional comment; do not lower an answer solely because checking found errors or disagreement. Do not convert missing information into No. No aggregate score.
